newsitem.title: UK: Mining shares look to better 1997 - fund manager.
newsitem.headline: Mining shares look to better 1997 - fund manager.

text.p: Mercury World Mining Trust Plc saw its share price fall 6.1 percent last year but the auguries are better for 1997, Graham Birch, the trust's investment manager, said on Tuesday.

The net asset value (NAV) fell 6.2 percent to 99.70 pence per share in 1996 but the world mining benchmark index lost 11.3 percent of its NAV last year, he said, adding that Mercury had outperformed the mining benchmark for about 20 months.
Nevertheless, the Mercury directors elected to increase the dividend by 15 percent due to the more favourable outlook in the mining sector, he told a briefing.
Already in 1997, prices of the metals mined by most of the companies in which Mercury had invested had improved. The mining trust is run by Mercury Asset Management.

On a March 7, 1997 year-end basis, the undiluted net asset value was showing a growth of 14.3 percent to 115.17 pence, against growth in the benchmark index of 11.7 percent, and the Mercury share price had gained nine percent.
It was last at 97 pence late on Tuesday.

Birch explained that for 1997, the Mercury share portfolio would outweigh the benchmark index in its holdings in South Africa (23 percent against 19 percent) and Latin America (11 percent against five percent).
It would be underweight against the index mainly in Europe, the U.S. and Canada.

Base metals shares would account for 45 percent of Mercury's portfolio this year against 23 percent in the benchmark index, and precious metals would account for 26 percent against 29 percent. Last year the precious metals share accounted for 37 percent of the portfolio.
"This is the first time we have been underweight in precious metals after three years of suffering," he said.

Most of the precious metals share would be in Harmony Gold Mining Co Ltd and Western Areas in South Africa. The low-cost Buenaventura Mining Co mine in Peru was the next largest precious metal aset, he said.
"Not only is Buenaventura a $100 per ounce cost mine but it has a very good exploration portfolio. We have made a lot of money out of it and expect to continue doing so," Birch said.
Zinc was the principal base metal covered in the portfolio, with the shares concentrated on Pasminco Ltd and Cominco Ltd.
Aluminum Co of America (ALCOA) was the principal aluminium stock held, due to its ability to reactivate previously idled capacity and produce intermediate aluminium products.
"Aluminium demand is now ahead of supply and the price is rising," Birch said.
There were three adverse factors affecting Mercury's performance last year, Birch said.

Gold prices lost ground from the first quarter onwards and although Mercury did not have a lot of copper exposure, it was still affected by huge price drop which followed the breaking of the Sumitomo Corp scandal which overflowed into the value of other metals.
"The second half of 1996 was worse than anyone had forecast," he said.
The third issue was sterling's strength against the U.S. dollar which took it from $1.49 to $1.71. This was "an adverse trend for us" as Mercury did not have its dollar income hedged.
Currency movements so far this year had been favourable, he said.

He argued that for 1997, base metals prices had turned upwards and and that the gold price may have bottomed out since dropping under $337.00 in February -- its lowest price since before the brief 1993 bull market.
"The base metals have been doing well with a pronounced rally and as the fundamentals are better, that should be sustainable," Birch said.
He cited the fall in London Metal Exchange (LME) warehouse stocks as an indication that the use of base metals was increasing in 1997.

He said Mercury was looking for a 3.50 percent growth in the OECD economies this year. "The economic trend tends to be a very good leading indicator (for metals prices). There is very good correlation," he said.
--Brian Spoors, London Newsroom +44 171 542 8058
